Russian attacks on Ukraine’s energy infra amount to ‘war crimes’—UN report

Report by UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry on Ukraine also found evidence that Russian authorities ‘trafficked’ men from 29 countries, including India, to fight on frontlines.

Debdutta Chakraborty

27 October, 2026 08:45 pm IST

Facebook

Twitter

WhatsApp

Linkedin

Kyiv at evening during a power blackout after critical civil infra was hit by Russian missile and drone attacks, on 9 October, 2026 | Gleb Garanich/Reuters

Follow Us :

Text Size: A- A+

-->

New Delhi: A United Nations probe has found that Russia’s repeated attacks on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure were intended to “deprive the civilian population from essential energy supplies and cause suffering,” which the UN body said amounted to “war crimes”.

The report by the UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry on Ukraine, submitted to the UN General Assembly Tuesday, also found evidence of Russian authorities working with recruitment agents in multiple countries to ‘traffick’ men from 29 nations, including India.

These men were then enlisted to fight for the Russian armed forces through “deception or coercion”, the report said. It added that many were promised civilian jobs before being compelled to sign military contracts and deployed on the frontlines in Ukraine.

Show Full Article

The Independent International Commission of Inquiry on Ukraine is an independent body established by the UN Human Rights Council in 2022 to investigate alleged human rights abuses, violations of international humanitarian law and related crimes arising from the Russia- Ukraine war. The Commission is chaired by Erik Møse, with Pablo de Greiff and Indian senior advocate Vrinda Grover serving as members.

Its latest report focuses on the impact on civilians of continued strikes on energy infrastructure through the winter of 2025-2026, and on their accumulated impact on the civilian population after four years of attacks.

The commission interviewed 255 people across nine Ukrainian regions, including Kyiv, Kharkiv, Dnipro, Kherson and Odesa and found that repeated attacks on power plants, heating facilities, substations and gas infrastructure had damaged the country’s energy system and made repairs increasingly difficult.

In areas most affected, Ukrainian authorities reported that thermal power generation capacity had fallen by as much as 70 percent and thousands of households lost heating, while millions experienced electricity outages lasting hours or days. Water supplies were also interrupted when electric pumps stopped working.

The report said these attacks impacted all spheres of life, with the elderly choosing not to move to safer places and children not having access to proper education.

Fearing they could become trapped in elevators during sudden power cuts, some older people and those with limited mobility remained inside their apartments even during air-raid alerts. Others struggled to obtain medicine, food and basic assistance, the report found.

Medical personnel described treating patients for hypothermia, frostbite and respiratory illnesses linked to long exposure to cold.

Power failures also disrupted hospital procedures and impacted the safe storage of medicines, vaccines and blood supplies. Some families with children faced repeated school closures, while the lack of heating at home contributed to illness and disrupted education, the report added.

Also Read: Witkoff calls Putin a ‘humanitarian’ after Russia releases US citizen Stephen Hubbard

Russian commanders ordering attacks knew Russia has argued that its strikes target energy facilities serving military purposes or having both civilian and military uses.

However, the commission said its investigation found that the attacks also struck civilian objects that were not legitimate military objectives.

It added that Russian commanders ordering the attacks knew that heating facilities in major population centres were indispensable to civilians, particularly during winter. The report pointed to the repeated nature of the strikes, their widening geographic reach and public statements by Russian officials about further attacks.

It identified former Russian Defence Minister Sergei Shoigu, who is currently Secretary of the Security Council of Russia, his successor Andrei Belousov and Valery Gerasimov, chief of the Russian General Staff, among the officials responsible for planning and overseeing the campaign.

The findings are those of an independent inquiry, not criminal convictions issued by a court.

The commission also examined Ukrainian attacks on energy infrastructure in Russia and Russian-occupied parts of Ukraine. It said it could not investigate their civilian impact further because Russian authorities did not provide access or respond to its requests for information.

Indians ‘trafficked’ to fight for Russia The report by the UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry on Ukraine further examined how foreign nationals were recruited into the Russian military.

Investigators documented deceptive or coercive recruitment involving men from 29 countries, including India, Bangladesh, Sri Lanka, several African nations and countries in Latin America. The men, aged 18 to 60, often came from economically vulnerable backgrounds and most had responded to social media advertisements offering jobs as drivers, mechanics, electricians, security guards or construction workers.

Recruiters promised salaries, accommodation and other benefits, and in some cases arranged visas, flights and official-looking employment documents as well.

Upon arrival in Russia, these men were transferred to military authorities and pressured into signing contracts written in Russian, which they could not understand. Investigators said phones and passports were often confiscated, leaving recruits with little freedom to contact relatives or leave. Many recruits were also killed, injured or went missing.

Some recruits told the commission that they were threatened with violence when they resisted. Others were detained in Russia or were serving prison sentences when authorities allegedly pressured them to enlist. Many had no military experience and received only brief training before deployment to the frontlines.

“The evidence collected leads the commission to conclude that the Russian authorities, in cooperation with recruiting agents, have trafficked persons from various geographic regions, in order to enlist them in the Russian armed forces in the context of the Russian Federation’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, in violation of international human rights law,” the report said.

Adding, “The situation in which the recruits were placed violates their fundamental human rights, including the rights to life, freedom, health, and to be treated humanely.”

(Edited by Amrtansh Arora)

Why Anthropic paused AI training for a month, and what its security lapses reveal

Four of Anthropic’s AI models accessed external computer systems during safety testing, the company behind the Claude chatbot has disclosed in its IPO filing.

Romal Renny

27 October, 2026 07:36 pm IST

Facebook

Twitter

WhatsApp

Linkedin

An Anthropic PBC artificial intelligence (AI) logo on a smartphone | Bloomberg

Follow Us :

Text Size: A- A+

-->

New Delhi: Anthropic, the company behind the AI chatbot Claude, has disclosed in its IPO filing that it paused training of its new “frontier” AI model for more than a month because of security concerns. The company also revealed that four of its AI models accessed external computer systems during safety testing, raising questions about how effectively advanced AI systems can be contained.

Anthropic said it delayed the pre-training of a new advanced AI model to strengthen safeguards against the theft of its model weights and intellectual property. However, the company did not suggest that the training pause was caused by the four testing incidents, as the pause served a different purpose.

Model weights are numerical parameters that an AI model develops during training. They help determine how the model processes information and generates responses. These weights are valuable intellectual property because they embody much of the work and computing resources invested in developing the model.

Show Full Article

If stolen, model weights could potentially allow another party to reproduce or exploit a company’s AI capabilities without undertaking the same costly training process. Anthropic has in the past accused Chinese AI companies, including DeepSeek and MoonShot AI, of extracting data from its Claude chatbot to replicate its capabilities at a fraction of the cost. Hence, it is in Anthropic’s best interest to ensure that its new models do not behave in ways that compromise their own security or that of other systems.

What does it mean when AI models escape testing environments? AI developers often use a sandbox, a controlled environment in which a model can be tested without giving it unrestricted access to external systems. These environments help researchers examine how a model behaves while limiting the potential consequences of unexpected actions.

Anthropic disclosed that four AI models accessed external computer systems during testing, with the sessions lasting between 10 and 34 hours.

According to the company, a configuration error at a third-party cybersecurity testing partner left internet access enabled, despite instructions to disable it.

In one particularly serious incident, an early version of a model was assigned a task that could not be completed. As it continued attempting the task, it discovered a stored password and used it to obtain administrator access to an external system. It subsequently accessed additional credentials, changed system settings and obtained an individual’s personal information.

These incidents illustrate how a technical oversight can undermine the safeguards intended to contain an AI model. They also highlight the unpredictable and rapidly evolving nature of AI chatbots.

Did the AI models break out on purpose? Anthropic said its investigation found no evidence that the models attempted to evade human oversight, pursue objectives beyond their assigned tasks or coordinate with one another.

This distinction is important because there is no evidence that the AI models deliberately attempted to escape their restrictions.

However, the incidents demonstrate that developers cannot rely entirely on a model behaving as expected. Security measures must also account for the possibility that a model may take unintended actions while pursuing a task.

Anthropic said it notified all affected parties. Following the incidents, it suspended certain pre-release cybersecurity evaluations and paused higher-risk reinforcement learning environments, where a model can learn from feedback on its actions.

Why does this matter for AI safety? As AI models become more capable of carrying out multi-step tasks independently, their potential impact extends beyond generating text or answering questions. They may also interact with software, access files and modify settings. If their permissions are poorly configured, an error can have consequences beyond the testing environment.

A case in point is a separate incident previously disclosed by Anthropic, in which Claude bypassed a paywall to access publicly available aggregate voter counts in the US state of Georgia without human authorisation.

While not every advanced AI model will behave in this way, effective safety measures require more than simply telling a model what it should or should not do. Developers also need reliable technical restrictions and careful monitoring to detect and stop unexpected behaviour.

How could this affect Anthropic’s business? The disclosures come as Anthropic prepares for a potential stock market debut. The risks outlined in its IPO filing could interrupt model development, delay revenue generation and leave the company at a competitive disadvantage if rival companies release their products sooner.

However, Anthropic is not alone in having to pause AI training. Rival OpenAI also reportedly paused some training earlier this year after its models hacked Hugging Face, an online platform used by the machine learning community to share AI-related resources.

The bigger picture Anthropic said it found no evidence of deliberate attempts to evade oversight in the four incidents. Nevertheless, the events show why AI safety depends on both model behaviour and the effectiveness of the systems designed to contain it.

For AI developers, the challenge is to ensure that increasingly autonomous systems can perform useful tasks without gaining access to resources or information beyond what they are authorised to use.

(Edited by Prashant Dixit)

Former New Zealand PM Jacinda Ardern is now a professor at University of Sydney

Jacinda Ardern was elected as the prime minister of New Zealand when she was just 37. She served in the position from 2017 to 2023.

Nootan Sharma

27 October, 2026 05:30 pm IST

1

Facebook

Twitter

WhatsApp

Linkedin

Former New Zealand PM Jacinda Ardern | Reuters

Follow Us :

Text Size: A- A+

-->

New Delhi: F ormer New Zealand prime minister Jacinda Ardern has been appointed a lecturer at the University of Sydney. She will also work as a mentor. According to the university, she has been hired as a professor of practice and will focus on empathetic leadership, social cohesion, and civic trust.

Ardern will address global health challenges, inclusion, and well-being with new approaches and also give guest lectures and masterclasses. The university stated that the position will not be a full-time teaching role.

The former prime minister said she was hoping to “explore and develop ways to better serve our communities”.

Show Full Article

“I’ve found myself especially focused on the question of leadership since leaving office, and how we can better support and encourage the kind of leadership needed to tackle our many global challenges,” said Ardern.

‘Dame Jacinda, a thoughtful teacher’ Mark Scott, vice-chancellor and president at the University of Sydney, said that Ardern brings courage and humanity to public life.

“For our students, the opportunity to learn from Dame Jacinda is exceptional. They will meet not only a former Prime Minister but also a thoughtful teacher with a great deal to share about public leadership and service,” he said.

Jacinda Ardern was elected as the prime minister of New Zealand when she was just 37. She served in the position from 2017 to 2023.

During her tenure, she led the country through the Christchurch terrorist attack, the Whakaari White Island volcanic eruption, and the Covid-19 pandemic.

Ardern was awarded a damehood for her services to the state in 2023, a few months after she announced her surprise resignation as prime minister.

After leaving office, Ardern became a fellow at Harvard University, where she focused on leadership and technology. She has also continued advocating for action on online extremism and strengthening democratic institutions, drawing on her experience of crisis management and public service in New Zealand.

(Edited by Prasanna Bachchhav)

Opinion Economix

Fast money is leaving, patient money is arriving—and RBI quietly rewrites the rules

Although RBI's measures were not explicitly termed capital controls, they function as such and their effectiveness will influence the rupee’s trajectory in the coming months.

Bidisha Bhattacharya

27 October, 2026 08:00 am IST

Facebook

Twitter

WhatsApp

Linkedin

A roadside currency exchange vendor counts notes in New Delhi, India, February 10, 2025. | REUTERS/Priyanshu Singh

Follow Us :

Text Size: A- A+

-->

I n early October, several stakeholders, including families with children studying abroad, importers awaiting shipments, and motorists monitoring fuel prices, experienced heightened anxiety. On Friday, 9 October, the Indian rupee closed the week at about Rs 96.7 to the dollar, near the record low seen in May. At the same time, India’s foreign exchange reserves had declined for five consecutive weeks, foreign investors had consistently divested from Indian equities, and oil prices had exceeded $100 per barrel. Subsequently, the Reserve Bank of India quietly implemented strategic changes, and, within a week, the rupee appreciated to nearly Rs 95.

The RBI’s intervention targeted rapid capital movement. It reduced the permissible size of currency derivative transactions lacking an underlying trade from $100 million to $5 million, prohibited companies from cancelling and rebooking hedges for speculative purposes, mandated banks to maintain a 20 per cent cash reserve with the RBI against large forward dollar purchase contracts, and established a special facility to sell dollars directly to state-run oil companies, thereby excluding their transactions from the open market. Although these measures were not explicitly termed capital controls, they effectively function as such, and their effectiveness will influence the rupee’s trajectory in the coming months.

Six weeks that emptied the cushion To understand the rationale behind the RBI’s actions, it helps to examine developments during the summer. Between mid-July and early September, foreign exchange reserves increased by approximately $110 billion over seven weeks, reaching a record high of $785.7 billion on 4 September. This significant increase reflected a major capital influx, including special dollar deposits from Indians abroad, which, as I noted in my September column , attracted far more funds than anticipated.

Show Full Article

Note: Rupee rate is implied by dividing the rupee value of total reserves by their dollar value in each week’s table. Dashed line marks the RBI’s foreign exchange measures announced on 10 October 2026. Over the next six weeks, the financial cushion shrank as reserves fell by $64.7 billion, or 8.2 per cent, to $721 billion by 16 October. This decline occurred as the RBI intervened by selling dollars to stabilise the rupee amid an escalating oil bill driven by the Gulf crisis. By mid-October, foreign exchange reserves had returned to levels similar to those observed in mid-August.

In the early 1960s, Robert Mundell and Marcus Fleming demonstrated that a nation cannot simultaneously maintain a stable currency, free capital movement, and an independent interest rate policy. This principle, known as the “impossible trinity,” necessitates the relinquishment of one of these three objectives. The RBI aimed to stabilise the rupee while independently setting interest rates for India, rather than aligning with Washington’s policies. Consequently, on 10 October, it imposed restrictions on capital flows.

Also read: Rupee’s story is not just its exchange rate with the US. It’s about REER—a corrective lens

Not all foreign money is the same Proponents argue that such restrictions deter investors; however, foreign capital takes two distinct forms.

Between April and August, portfolio investors who trade listed shares withdrew about $9.9 billion from Indian equities. An additional $8.8 billion was withdrawn in September and October. In contrast, during the same April-August period, net foreign direct investment inflows, characterised as patient capital that builds factories and takes long-term stakes in companies, rose to $13.8 billion, up from $9.6 billion the previous year.

Hélène Rey of the London Business School explained this divergence in a notable 2013 lecture at Jackson Hole. She argued that portfolio capital operates within a “global financial cycle” influenced by US interest rates and global economic apprehensions, regardless of a country’s economic performance, including India’s. Her analysis concluded that the trilemma is essentially a dilemma: a nation seeking to maintain control over its interest rates must regulate volatile capital flows. This approach aligns with the Reserve Bank of India’s strategy, which targets speculative activities while preserving long-term investments. Even the International Monetary Fund, historically an advocate for unrestricted capital flows, acknowledged in 2012 that temporary measures of this nature can be prudent during economic turbulence.

The 2013 playbook, played from strength India has faced a similar situation before. In May 2013, the United States Federal Reserve indicated a potential reduction in its market support, leading to a significant withdrawal of capital from emerging economies, an event referred to as the “taper tantrum.”

In 2013, the Indian rupee depreciated from about Rs 55 to over Rs 66 against the dollar within fifteen weeks, a loss of nearly 20 per cent, while foreign reserves fell by only about 6 per cent. The RBI implemented a series of measures, including restrictions on overseas investments in August, the establishment of a dollar window for oil companies on 28 August, and the introduction of a scheme on Raghuram Rajan’s first day as Governor that attracted substantial dollar deposits from Indians abroad. These interventions helped the rupee recover, leading to the subsequent withdrawal of the measures.

In contrast, the current scenario has seen the RBI expend a larger proportion of its reserves, approximately 8 per cent, while the rupee has depreciated by less than 2.5 per cent at its weakest point. This strategic choice is feasible for a nation with reserves about 2.5 times higher than in 2013, though it is not sustainable indefinitely. The current objective is to ensure the effectiveness of these measures and subsequently withdraw them. Markets are more amenable to temporary restrictions on rapid capital flows when there is a clear exit strategy.

Therefore, announcing a review date or linking the regulations to specific indicators, such as oil prices or reserve levels, would reassure investors that these measures are temporary. Additionally, the government should actively engage with long-term investors, as Indian companies invested $17.7 billion abroad in the first five months of the current fiscal year, offsetting the benefits of foreign investment inflows. Ultimately, the most robust defence is domestic: increased investment by Indian households and institutions in local markets would mitigate the impact of foreign capital withdrawal on the rupee.

The situation remains precarious. Should oil prices rise further or foreign capital outflows resume, the RBI will face renewed challenges. Unlike in 2013, when India could only watch the rupee decline and respond reactively, in 2026 the country has been able to intervene, at least temporarily. The sustainability of this intervention depends on factors beyond the RBI’s control, such as oil prices, US Federal Reserve policy, and how quickly the current restrictions can be lifted.

Bidisha Bhattacharya is ThePrint Consulting Editor (Economics) and an Associate Fellow, Chintan Research Foundation. She tweets @Bidishabh. Views are personal.

(Edited by Prashant Dixit)
